summary:
Moonbase Blackout is an interactive, browser-based lunar survival game that teaches children ages 7–12 how to make engineering decisions with limited resources.

Built for NASA Space Apps' Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, the game puts players in charge of a fictional Moon base during a 36-hour power blackout. With one battery and six shifts, players must balance life support, greenhouse lighting, and crew protection. Every choice costs energy, and planning ahead determines whether the mission succeeds.

The game uses a real May 2024 solar energetic particle observation from NASA's DONKI archive. A fictional mission clock maps this data to a critical warning, making NASA data part of a decision players must act on. Different choices lead to different outcomes, with mission reports explaining the consequences.

Early playtesting with children revealed that the prototype lacked engagement. Their feedback led to clearer controls, stronger warnings, and more visible consequences.

Moonbase Blackout helps young learners practice prioritizing safety, managing limited resources, and planning for future needs. These are skills that matter in space exploration and everyday problem-solving.
details:
What We Developed

Moonbase Blackout is a free, browser-based educational game designed to introduce children ages 7–12 to the engineering challenges of living and working on the Moon. Created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge, it transforms complex space-mission decisions into an interactive survival experience where every choice has consequences.

Players become responsible for a fictional lunar outpost experiencing a 36-hour solar-power blackout. They must protect their crew, maintain essential life support, provide enough light for greenhouse plants, and conserve limited energy until solar power returns.

How the Game Works

The mission begins with a 92 kWh battery and six shifts lasting six hours each. Players choose one of three commands per shift:

  • Conserve (12 kWh): Maintain essential life support while saving energy.
  • Greenhouse (18 kWh): Maintain life support and provide one period of light for plants.
  • Shelter (18 kWh): Maintain life support and protect the crew during a dangerous particle event.

The greenhouse needs two light periods, and the crew must enter Shelter during a specific warning. Spending too much energy early can jeopardize later decisions.

The game features an illustrated lunar environment, interactive command console, animated system responses, visible resource indicators, multiple outcomes, and educational mission reports. Players can retry the mission, experiment with different strategies, and discover why their decisions succeeded or failed.

Meaningful NASA Data Integration

The game incorporates a real, archived solar energetic particle (SEP) observation from NASA's DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information).

The observation, recorded on May 11, 2024, is mapped into the game's fictional mission clock using a defined time offset. Its timestamp determines when a solar-particle warning appears before Shift 3.

This makes NASA data an active part of gameplay rather than merely background information: players must recognize the warning, reserve sufficient energy, and activate Shelter at the correct time.

The simulation deliberately simplifies real engineering systems. Its battery, blackout, greenhouse requirements, and shelter mechanics are fictional educational models, not representations of actual lunar habitat specifications. The historical observation is not a live lunar radiation forecast. These distinctions, along with source references and the timing calculation, are documented in the game's Behind the Mission section.

Educational Impact and Creativity

Our goal is to help children develop critical thinking, resource management, prioritization, and forward planning through hands-on problem-solving.

Rather than simply presenting facts about space exploration, Moonbase Blackout lets players experience the consequences of engineering trade-offs. Protecting the crew is essential, but success also requires anticipating future needs and allocating limited resources effectively.

The game was refined using feedback from children in a community STEM, business, and leadership program. An early prototype functioned correctly but was described as boring. This feedback prompted improvements to the interface, mission storytelling, visual consequences, warnings, and educational reports.

The resulting experience combines a mission-control-inspired interface, simple resource-management mechanics, real NASA archive data, and interactive storytelling. Its intended applications include classrooms, STEM workshops, and independent learning. Further playtesting will be needed to measure educational outcomes.

Technology, Development, and Validation

Moonbase Blackout was built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript ES modules, and original SVG artwork, with GitHub Pages providing free public hosting. The game requires no installation, account, backend, or specialized hardware. Node.js was used for automated testing.

The simulation passed 11 automated tests covering resource calculations, warning timing, successful and unsuccessful outcomes, input handling, and retry behaviour. These tests establish consistency in the game mechanics, not scientific validation of real lunar systems.

Luqman led the concept, research, learning objectives, game design, engineering requirements, UI/UX direction, child-feedback integration, testing, and iteration. Farhan contributed technical advice and code review.

AI assistance was used transparently: ChatGPT supported research, planning, and review, while OpenAI Codex contributed to implementation, development, debugging, testing, and documentation. Luqman directed project decisions, requirements, development, evaluation, and iteration.

Intended Impact

Moonbase Blackout demonstrates that meaningful engineering education does not require complicated equipment or advanced mathematics. By making resource constraints and consequences visible, it aims to spark curiosity about space exploration and help young learners understand a fundamental engineering principle:

Successful missions depend not only on what we can do, but on deciding what matters most, what can wait, and how today's choices affect tomorrow's possibilities.

Play the game: https://luqman338.github.io/Moonbase-blackout/

Explore the code and documentation: https://github.com/luqman338/Moonbase-blackout
